content:
A list circulating on social media, titled "Before you convert to Islam", gives a would-be convert a set of "roles" to accept first. Several concern women. It tells the convert to "treat women inferiorly" and "always believe that men are superior".

It says a woman convert "need[s] to be circumcised", must decide whether she can "cope being a minor wife", and must cover almost her whole body, while modest dress for a man is "almost unnecessary". It adds separation of the sexes, a ban on romance because "instant marriage is recommended", and an instruction to "justify child marriage".

Some of these items describe real teachings in distorted form, and some have no basis in the sources at all. This article aims to provide context to the list's claims about women and marriage, insha'Allah, in seven answers. A companion article takes up what a convert actually takes on, and another the list's claims about apostates and LGBT friends.

The Quran frames the question of worth in one verse: "O mankind, indeed We have created you from male and female and made you peoples and tribes that you may know one another. Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you" (49:13).[1]

The list's ninth and tenth "minor roles" are "Treat women inferiorly" and "Always believe that men are superior". The Quran measures every person by righteousness (49:13). It says that men and women were created "from one soul" (4:1), and it promises reward for good deeds "whether male or female" (16:97).[1]

When the believers prayed, the Quran records God's answer: "Never will I allow to be lost the work of [any] worker among you, whether male or female; you are of one another" (3:195).[1] Verse 33:35 lists ten virtues, from faith to remembrance of God, and names "Muslim men and Muslim women" for each, with the same forgiveness and reward for both.[1]

The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "The best of you is the best to his wives, and I am the best of you to my wives."[2] Asked a question of ritual purity about women, he answered that the rule was the same, because "women are counterparts of men".[3] A convert who treated women as inferior would be disobeying both texts.

The Prophet's conduct at home matched his words. When ʿĀʾisha was asked what he did in his house, she said: "He used to keep himself busy serving his family and when it was the time for prayer he would go for it."[4] The man whom Muslims take as their model did the work of his own household.

The list's claim has a real text behind it, and we state it plainly. Verse 4:34 says: "Men are in charge of women by [right of] what Allah has given one over the other and what they spend [for maintenance] from their wealth".[1] The verse gives the husband charge of the household and ties it to his duty to provide for it.

That charge is a responsibility within marriage. The same Quran says that "the believing men and believing women are allies of one another" (9:71) and commands husbands, "live with them in kindness" (4:19).[1] It describes marriage as "affection and mercy" (30:21).[1]

The ranking that matters is the one 49:13 gives, by righteousness, and it is open to both sexes on the same terms. We set out the rest of the law, on testimony and inheritance, in our article on women in Islamic law.

The list says a woman convert "need[s] to be circumcised". The classical record is mixed, and we state it as it is. Al-Nawawī reports that the Shāfiʿī school held circumcision obligatory for men and women, while Mālik and Abū Ḥanīfa held it a sunna for both, and a minority view within his own school made it obligatory for men only.[5]

The only report cited for women is the hadith of Umm ʿAṭiyya, in which the Prophet told a woman who circumcised girls in Medina not to cut severely. Abū Dāwūd, who records it, judged it himself: "It is not a strong tradition", and "this tradition is weak".[6] Al-Nawawī repeats Abū Dāwūd's judgement, and the jurists who allowed the practice still limited it to the least that the name could apply to.[5]

Modern authorities have gone further. In 2007 the Grand Mufti of Egypt, ʿAlī Jumʿa, said that the practice is "not supported by the Quran or Islamic law" and that "this custom is harmful and it is forbidden".[7]

Egypt's Dār al-Iftāʾ calls the evidence for it "extremely weak", notes that the Prophet did not have his own daughters circumcised, and says that its prohibition "is in accord with the objectives of Islamic law".[8] No convert is required to undergo it.

The list tells a woman convert to ask whether she can "cope being a minor wife", and a man whether he is "wealthy to have 4 or more wives". The Quran permits a man to marry up to four wives, and no more. It attaches a condition at once: "But if you fear that you will not be just, then [marry only] one" (4:3).[1]

It then warns: "And you will never be able to be equal [in feeling] between wives, even if you should strive [to do so]. So do not incline completely [toward one] and leave another hanging" (4:129).[1] A man who takes a second wife takes on that burden of justice, and the law treats each wife as a wife, with her own rights. The phrase "minor wife" comes from the list, and no source uses it.

A woman is not obliged to accept polygyny either. Marriage in Islam requires her consent, as the Prophet said: "a virgin should not be given in marriage except after her permission".[9] Under Egyptian law, for example, a couple may agree in the marriage contract that the husband will take no second wife.[10]

The list says that a woman must cover almost her whole body and wear a hijab, and that for a man modest dress "is almost unnecessary". The Quran's command on modesty begins with men. "Tell the believing men to reduce [some] of their vision and guard their private parts. That is purer for them" (24:30).[1]

Only then does it turn to women, with the same two commands and the further instruction "to wrap [a portion of] their headcovers over their chests" (24:31).[1] Dress is given to both sexes "to conceal your private parts and as adornment. But the clothing of righteousness - that is best" (7:26).[1] The Prophet said that "Haya' is a part of faith", and he said it of a man.[11]

The rules of dress differ between men and women. The duty of modesty does not belong to one of them. We set out the verses on women's dress in our article on hijab and modesty.

The list tells the convert to "be separate to different gender". The sources forbid a man and a woman who are not close relatives to be alone together: "No man should stay with a lady in seclusion except in the presence of a Dhu-Mahram".[12]

They do not shut women out of public life. The Prophet said: "Do not stop Allah's women-slaves from going to Allah's Mosques".[13]

The list also says a convert should avoid romantic relationships "because instant marriage is recommended". The Quran forbids sex outside marriage: "do not approach unlawful sexual intercourse. Indeed, it is ever an immorality" (17:32).[1] The command binds men and women alike. The Prophet encouraged young people to marry if they were able, "because it helps him lower his gaze and guard his modesty", and to fast if they were not.[14]

That is encouragement to marry, with a fallback for those who cannot, and marriage still needs the consent of both.[9]

The list's last "minor role" is "Justify child marriage". A convert enters Islam by the testimony of faith, and nothing in that testimony obliges him to defend any practice. The Quran ties marriage to maturity: orphans are tested "until they reach marriageable age", and their property is released to them when they show "sound judgement" (4:6).[1]

Marriage requires the bride's permission, as the Prophet said in the report already cited.[9] When Khansāʾ bint Khidhām's father married her to a man she disliked, she went to the Prophet, "and he declared that marriage invalid".[15] A marriage made without the bride's consent did not stand. Muslim-majority states today set minimum ages for marriage in their own laws. We set out the classical rulings, the debate over ʿĀʾisha's age and the modern laws in our article on child marriage in Islam.

The bottom line

The list tells converts to treat women as inferior. The Quran measures every person by righteousness, creates men and women from one soul, and promises the same reward to both. The husband's charge in 4:34 is tied to his duty to provide, and it sits beside commands to kindness and mutual support.

Female circumcision rests on a report that its own compiler called weak, and Egypt's Grand Mufti and Dār al-Iftāʾ have declared it forbidden. Polygyny is a permission bounded by justice, and a woman may refuse it. Modesty is commanded to men before women, and marriage needs the consent of both.

A convert who takes on Islam takes on these texts, which ask more of a man toward women than the list ever mentions. God knows best.

Notes

  1. Quran 49:13; 4:1; 16:97; 3:195; 33:35; 4:34; 9:71; 4:19; 30:21; 4:3; 4:129; 24:30; 24:31; 7:26; 17:32; 4:6, Saheeh International translation.
  2. Jami al-Tirmidhi 3895, report of ʿĀʾisha, graded sahih by Aḥmad Shākir and al-Albānī.
  3. Sunan Abī Dāwūd 236, report of ʿĀʾisha, graded hasan by al-Albānī.
  4. Sahih al-Bukhari 676, report of al-Aswad from ʿĀʾisha.
  5. Al-Nawawī, al-Majmūʿ sharḥ al-Muhadhdhab (Beirut: Dār al-Fikr), vol. 1, pp. 300–301, in the OpenITI text of the Shamela edition.
  6. Sunan Abī Dāwūd 5271, report of Umm ʿAṭiyya al-Anṣāriyya, with Abū Dāwūd's comments. Al-Albānī later graded it sahih.
  7. "Egypt Mufti defends ban on female genital cutting", Daily News Egypt, 7 July 2007, https://www.dailynewsegypt.com/2007/07/07/egypt-mufti-defends-ban-on-female-genital-cutting/, quoting ʿAlī Jumʿa's interview with Reuters.
  8. Dār al-Iftāʾ al-Miṣriyya, "Female circumcision contradicts Islamic law", https://www.dar-alifta.org/en/article/details/1881/female-circumcision-contradicts-islamic-law.
  9. Sahih al-Bukhari 5136, report of Abū Hurayra.
  10. Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (UK), "Family law in Egypt", updated 29 October 2025, https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/family-law-in-egypt/family-law-in-egypt--2.
  11. Sahih al-Bukhari 24, report of ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar.
  12. Sahih al-Bukhari 5233, report of Ibn ʿAbbās.
  13. Sahih al-Bukhari 900, report of Ibn ʿUmar.
  14. Sahih al-Bukhari 5066, report of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd.
  15. Sahih al-Bukhari 5138, report of Khansāʾ bint Khidhām al-Anṣāriyya.
